problems.memo_sentence: "The paper frames quantum speedups for solving NP-hard mixed-integer optimization problems via Branch-and-Bound and Branch-and-Cut, and more generally heuristic tree search, with application examples including Mean-Variance Portfolio Optimization alongside the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model and Maximum Independent Set."
problems.source_evidence: The paper says: "We use numerical simulation to verify that Q ≫ d for typical instances of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, Maximum Independent Set, and Mean-Variance Portfolio Optimization; as well as to extrapolate the dependence of Q on input size parameters."
problems.explanation: This is not a claim from another cited paper, but the memo slightly misstates the portfolio example as "alongside" the others in the abstract framing. More importantly, the paper’s portfolio benchmark is specifically "Mean-Variance Portfolio Optimization with diversification constraints," which the memo later treats as a generic portfolio optimization setting.

problems.memo_sentence: "The authors define universal speedup as preserving any instance-specific ‘luck’ of a classical algorithm, so the quantum algorithm is at least as fast up to a near-quadratic improvement over the empirically realized classical query complexity Q(ε)."
problems.source_evidence: The paper says: "if a classical Branch-and-Bound algorithm has complexity Q on an instance that leads to solution depth d, Incremental-Quantum-Branch-and-Bound offers the same guarantees with a complexity of ˜O(√Qd)." It also says the speedup is over the actual performance of the classical algorithm "in every case" and that the quantum algorithm depends on the heuristic used classically.
problems.explanation: The memo omits the explicit dependence on solution depth d and the fact that the guarantee is stated relative to a classical algorithm on an instance, not simply to an empirical query complexity Q(ε) alone. That makes the speedup statement stronger and less qualified than the source.

problems.memo_sentence: "Their framework restricts attention to Branch-Local heuristics, including depth-first, cost-based, and A* strategies, and reduces general heuristics to local ones under simplifying assumptions such as binary trees, integer-valued cost functions, and distinct heuristic rankings."
problems.source_evidence: The paper explicitly says: "The family of heuristics in Deﬁnition 1.2 is probably broader than needed to include all search methods used in practice... Nevertheless, it is possible that some Branch-and-Bound algorithm uses a heuristic that does not fall under this deﬁnition and such algorithms will not be covered by our results."
problems.explanation: The memo does not reflect the paper’s explicit limitation that some practical heuristics may fall outside the Branch-Local class and therefore are not covered. This is a substantive boundary on applicability.

problems.memo_sentence: "The authors acknowledge that their branch-and-cut quantum speedup may fail when more than an exponential number of global cutting planes are used, so the advantage is not universal over arbitrary cut-generation strategies."
problems.source_evidence: The paper says: "Observe that Theorem 1.4 introduces an additional dependence on p and so the algorithm may not have an advantage when more than an exponential number of global cutting planes are used."
problems.explanation: The memo captures the broad idea, but it misses the paper’s stronger point that the dependence is on the number of global cuts p and that the algorithm’s advantage may disappear specifically because of this extra p factor. The limitation is more concrete than the memo conveys.

problems.memo_sentence: "Numerical simulations on SK, MIS, and portfolio optimization instances show that for typical cases the depth scales at most quadratically with the number of nodes (d = O(n²)), classical node counts scale as O(2^{0.494n}) for SK, O(2^{0.0339n}) for MIS, and O(2^{0.195n}) for portfolio optimization, and that there are large spreads in performance across instances, supporting the relevance of universal speedup guarantees."
problems.source_evidence: The paper reports these as empirical fits from classical solver runs: "We obtained a measured complexity of O(20.494n) with r2 > 0.998 for the results obtained with Gurobi..." and similarly for MIS and portfolio optimization. It also says the depth metric from Gurobi "may not be an exact estimate of the true maximum depth" and is only assumed to be a valid approximation.
problems.explanation: The memo presents the fitted exponents as established properties of the problems rather than empirical regressions from specific solver runs. It also omits the caveat that the depth measure is only an approximation from solver logs.

problems.source_evidence: The paper’s Section 3 contains a substantial numerical study on SK, MIS, and portfolio optimization, including fitted scaling laws and performance spreads.
problems.explanation: The memo’s future-work entry says nothing, but the paper does include a significant empirical section. This is not a factual error about future work per se, but it reflects a strong bias toward the abstract/introduction and misses the paper’s results section entirely.
